title: What a Sport Is
description: In Signature terms, a sport is a contest with a shape: a field or course, a set of moves that count, a way of keeping score, and a finish line everyone can see. The shape is what turns raw effort into a fair test, because two athletes who have never met can step into the same rules and be compared honestly. A good sport rewards practice in a visible way, so training changes the result instead of merely changing the story told about it. It also protects the players, because rules that limit dangerous contact and demand honest play keep the contest going season after season. That is why a sport is more than exercise: exercise improves the body, while a sport tests the body and mind against other people under rules all sides accept.

demo.code:
teams = 2
sides = 11
print('Sides in a soccer match:', teams)
print('Players per side:', sides)
print('Total players on the field:', teams * sides)
demo.expected_output:
Sides in a soccer match: 2
Players per side: 11
Total players on the field: 22

history: People have played organised games for thousands of years, from running races and wrestling in ancient cultures to the codified team games of the nineteenth century.
rules: A sport is a physical contest played under agreed rules, with a defined way to score, a defined playing area or course, and officials or conventions that settle disputes.
techniques: Players learn the basic movements of their sport first, then combine them into tactics, and finally practise them under pressure so they hold up in competition.

title: The History of Sport
description: The long story of sport runs from village games to world championships, and the turning point was writing the rules down. Before codification, a game in one town could differ sharply from the same game in the next, so matches between strangers were hard to settle fairly. Once associations published a shared rulebook, a team could travel, play, and trust the result, and that trust is what allowed leagues and cups to grow. The ancient festivals matter because they show that organised contests with prizes and crowds are not a modern invention, but the modern system matters because it made those contests repeatable, comparable, and open to anyone who could meet the standard. A player today stands at the end of both lines: an old human love of contest, and a newer system that keeps that contest honest.

print('Ancient festival site: Olympia')
print('Modern Olympic revival year:', 1896)
print('Paralympic Games first held:', 1960)
print('Gap in years:', 1960-1896)

history: Ancient Olympic games were held at Olympia in Greece, and ball games, wrestling, and running contests appear in many early civilisations on every continent.
competitions: Modern sport took its present form when clubs, national associations, and international federations wrote common rules and organised regular championships.
statistics: No single date marks the birth of sport; instead, each sport has its own documented codification date, and this record gives those dates only where the sport's own federation records them.

title: The Olympic Movement
description: The Olympic idea is simple and demanding: bring the world's athletes together, under one set of rules, and let the contest speak. The modern revival in Athens in 1896 gave that idea a regular home, a four-year rhythm, and a host city that must build and prepare for guests from every continent. Behind the spectacle sits unglamorous work: federations agreeing on rules, judges trained to a common standard, and anti-doping checks applied to winners and also-rans alike. The ceremonies matter because they mark the meeting as something larger than a set of results, but the heart of the movement stays the same as any local meet: athletes, a fair start, and a finish that everyone can trust.

print('Cycle:', 4, 'years')
print('Editions in a 12-year span:', 12 // 4 * 2)

history: The modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896, revived by Pierre de Coubertin, and have since been held every four years except when cancelled by world wars.
competitions: The Games bring together athletes in summer and winter editions, with host cities chosen years in advance and sports added or removed by the International Olympic Committee.
rules: Olympic competition follows each sport federation's rules, with eligibility, anti-doping, and fair-play rules applying across all sports.

title: The Paralympic Movement
description: Paralympic sport starts from a different question than most sport histories ask. Instead of asking which bodies fit the game, it asks how the game can be shaped so that more bodies can play it at full intensity. Its roots lie in rehabilitation sport at Stoke Mandeville in 1948, where competition proved to be part of recovery, and its growth into the Rome Games of 1960 showed that this was not therapy alone but elite sport in its own right. Classification is the key invention: by grouping athletes by function, it makes results meaningful instead of merely inspiring. Adapted equipment, guides, and rule changes are not extras added to a normal sport; they are the sport, designed with the same care as any rulebook.

demo.code:
print('First Games: Rome 1960')

print('Growth in years from origin to first Games:', 1960-1948)
demo.expected_output:
First Games: Rome 1960
Stoke Mandeville origin: 1948
Growth in years from origin to first Games: 12

history: The Paralympic Games grew from the Stoke Mandeville Games for athletes with spinal injuries, first held in 1948, and became a parallel Games movement in 1960 in Rome.
rules: Paralympic athletes are classified by impairment so that competition is fair between athletes with similar functional ability.
safety: Classification, adapted equipment, and trained guides and pilots let athletes with a wide range of impairments compete safely at elite level.

title: How Sport Is Governed
description: Governance is the plumbing of sport: invisible when it works, obvious when it fails. The international federation holds the rulebook, the national body runs the domestic pyramid, and the club is where a player actually turns up on a wet evening. Each layer has a job the others cannot do: only the federation can make a rule binding worldwide, only the national body can run a fair national cup, and only the club can coach a beginner week after week. When the layers cooperate, a child can start at a local club and climb, step by step, to national competition without ever leaving the same rulebook. When they do not, fixtures clash, money leaks, and players lose trust in results, which is why transparent elections, published rules, and independent discipline matter as much as any trophy.

demo.expected_output:

rules: Each sport has an international federation that writes its rules, while national federations run domestic leagues and select national teams, and clubs are where most players belong.
competitions: Leagues, cups, and championships are organised in pyramids, so a local club can in principle rise through promotion to the top division.
history: Governing bodies grew from nineteenth-century associations that codified rules so that matches between strangers could be played fairly.

title: Amateur and Professional Sport
description: The amateur-professional line is about time and money, not about worth. An amateur gives evenings and weekends and plays for the love of it; a professional gives the whole working week and is paid because spectators, sponsors, or broadcasters value the contest. The old argument that pay spoils sport has faded, because full-time training is what makes elite standards possible, but the amateur game has not faded with it: it is where most people play, where volunteers run clubs, and where professionals themselves usually began. A healthy sport keeps both doors open, with clear rules for moving between them, so that talent is not trapped by income and enjoyment is not priced out by the professional game.

history: Early modern sport prized the amateur, who played for love of the game, while professional sport grew as crowds paid to watch the best players and clubs paid them to play.
competitions: Professional leagues sell tickets and broadcast rights and pay players, while amateur competitions rely on volunteers, membership fees, and grants.
training: Professionals train full-time with coaches, analysts, and medical staff; amateurs fit training around work or study.

title: Youth Sport
description: Youth sport succeeds when it treats children as players, not as small adults. The best sessions are short, busy, and joyful: small fields, smaller balls, many touches, and games where everyone plays rather than watches. Winning matters less at this stage than learning to move well, to listen to a coach, and to cope with losing without quitting. Adults carry the safety burden: qualified coaching, age-appropriate equipment, and safeguarding rules that keep the environment trustworthy. A child who enjoys sport at ten is far more likely to be active at thirty, and that lifelong habit is the real prize of youth sport, ahead of any trophy a single team might win.

training: Youth coaching emphasises fun, basic movement, and small-sided games, with competition introduced gradually as children grow.
safety: Safeguarding, qualified coaches, age-group rules, and appropriate equipment sizes protect young players.
techniques: Children learn best by playing: short practices, many touches of the ball, and games that let every child take part.

title: Women in Sport
description: The story of women in sport is a story of doors forced open. Early competitions excluded women outright, so women built their own clubs and cups and proved, match by match, that the exclusion had no sporting basis. Legal and policy changes then opened school and university sport, and professional women's leagues followed, with crowds and broadcasts growing as the quality and investment rose together. The remaining gaps are measurable and ordinary: pay, prize money, facilities, and airtime still lag behind the men's game in many sports, even where the women's competition is well established. Closing those gaps is not a favour to women's sport; it is the completion of the same fairness principle that governs every other part of sport.

print('Early exclusion: women barred from most first modern Games events')

print('Remaining gaps: pay, prizes, coverage in many sports')
demo.expected_output:

history: Women were long excluded from many competitions, including early Olympic events, and fought for entry, funding, and media coverage through the twentieth century.
competitions: Women's leagues, cups, and championships now run in most major sports, with professional women's leagues growing in soccer, basketball, cricket, and tennis.
statistics: Participation and audience figures for women's sport have grown sharply in recent years, though pay and coverage gaps remain in many sports.

title: Sport and Health
description: Health is the quiet argument for sport, stronger than any medal table. A body that runs, jumps, lifts, and balances regularly keeps its heart, lungs, muscles, and bones in better working order, and a mind that trains with others gains routine, friendship, and proof of progress. The catch is dosage: too little does nothing, too much too soon causes injury, and the right amount is built by warming up, progressing gradually, and resting between hard efforts. Coaches and clinicians both say the same thing in different words: consistency beats intensity, and a sport a person enjoys is a sport they will still be playing in ten years. That long view is what turns a game into a health habit.

training: Regular sport improves heart and lung fitness, strength, flexibility, balance, and coordination, and supports mental health through routine, social contact, and achievement.
safety: Health benefits depend on sensible loading: warm-ups, gradual progression, rest days, and early attention to pain or injury.
statistics: Health guidance in many countries recommends regular moderate activity for adults and children, with sport one of the most enjoyable ways to reach it.

title: Sport Science
description: Sport science turns coaching hunches into checkable claims. A stopwatch says how fast, a force plate says how hard, a heart-rate trace says how costly, and a recovery score says whether the athlete is ready to go again. Put together, those measures let a coach plan a week instead of merely reacting to it: hard days, easy days, and rest placed where the body can actually absorb them. Video and wearables add the detail the eye misses in real time, and sleep, food, and mindset complete the picture, because performance is a whole person, not a single muscle. The science earns its keep when it changes a decision: a load reduced, a technique corrected, a rest day taken before injury forces one.

print('Distance:', dist, 'm')

training: Sport scientists measure speed, power, endurance, and recovery, and use the numbers to plan training loads and rest.
techniques: Video analysis, wearable trackers, and force plates let coaches see what the eye misses and correct technique precisely.
safety: Load monitoring and screening help spot fatigue and injury risk before a small problem becomes a season-ending one.

title: Coaching
description: A coach is a teacher whose classroom is a field, a court, or a pool. The work starts before practice, in planning a season and breaking a complex skill into steps a beginner can actually perform. During practice, the coach demonstrates, gives one clear correction at a time, and asks questions that make athletes notice their own errors instead of merely obeying orders. Off the field, the coach selects fairly, communicates honestly with players and parents, and protects the team's culture, so that effort is valued and setbacks are treated as information. Wins are the visible measure, but the deeper measure is whether athletes leave the season better, keener, and more likely to return next year.

print('Total sets:', squad * sets)

training: Coaches plan seasons, design practices, teach skills step by step, and give feedback that athletes can act on.
techniques: Good coaching mixes demonstration, short clear instructions, guided practice, and questions that make athletes think for themselves.
history: Coaching qualifications now run in most sports, with levels from beginner helper to elite performance coach.

title: Officiating and Fair Play
description: Fair play needs a person in the middle, not just a rulebook on a shelf. Officials are trained to stand where they can see, to signal so everyone understands, and to decide quickly while players and crowds press for the opposite call. Their authority is what lets rivals accept a result they dislike, and that acceptance is the foundation of every league table. Video review helps in some sports by catching what the eye missed, but it cannot supply judgement about intent, advantage, or the spirit of the game. The ethic around officiating matters just as much: players who own their fouls, coaches who accept decisions, and crowds who do not abuse officials keep the contest civil enough to be worth playing.

rules: Referees, umpires, and judges enforce the rules, keep time, record scores, and decide contested incidents, with video review assisting in some sports.
history: Officiating grew with codified sport: once rules were written, someone had to apply them neutrally, and training and assessment followed.
techniques: Officials train in positioning, signalling, communication, and decision-making under pressure, and are assessed after matches.

title: Ethics in Sport
description: Ethics is the question that remains after the rulebook runs out. Rules can forbid a foul, but only an ethic can ask whether winning by deception is worth anything, and the answer sport gives is no: a bought or faked result destroys the meaning of every honest result around it. The ethic covers more than cheating: it covers respect for rivals and officials, inclusion of people who have historically been shut out, honest eligibility, and the adult duty to protect young players from pressure that serves a club more than a child. Codes and tribunals back the ethic up, but they cannot create it; it is created match by match, when a player owns a foul, a coach refuses a fix, and a crowd applauds good play from either side.

demo.expected_output:
Competing well means more than winning

rules: Sporting ethics cover honesty, respect, inclusion, and the duty of adults to protect young and vulnerable participants.
history: Ethical codes grew as sport professionalised and money and media pressure created new temptations to cheat or fix results.
competitions: Match-fixing, bribery, and deliberately losing are banned in every major sport and can end careers and bring criminal penalties in some countries.

title: Doping and Anti-Doping
description: Anti-doping exists because performance drugs break sport twice over: once by cheating rivals, and once by harming the user. The global system centres on a yearly prohibited list, testing in and out of competition, and stored samples that can be retested when detection catches up with new drugs. Penalties are severe, including long suspensions and stripped results, because a single doped result distorts rankings, prize money, and selection for everyone else. Athletes carry strict responsibility for their own bodies, so a banned ingredient in an ordinary supplement or medicine is no defence, and checking before taking anything is part of being a professional. The health case is just as plain: many banned substances damage heart, liver, and hormones, turning a short advantage into a long risk.

rules: Doping is the use of banned substances or methods to improve performance, and anti-doping rules ban them, test athletes, and punish violations.
safety: Many banned substances carry serious health risks, including heart, liver, and hormonal damage, which is one reason they are banned.
history: Modern anti-doping began with testing at major Games and grew into the World Anti-Doping Agency and a global code adopted by federations.

title: Sport Media and Broadcasting
description: Broadcasting changed sport by changing who could watch it. Radio let a listener follow a match from home, television let a viewer see a replay and a tactic in slow motion, and streaming lets a fan choose a device, an angle, and a live statistic feed. That reach brings money: rights sales fund wages, grounds, and in some leagues grassroots work, but they also move kick-off times and shape calendars around audiences rather than players. The best coverage does more than show the game; it teaches it, with commentary and graphics that explain why a substitution or a formation change mattered. The risk is the opposite: coverage that treats sport as background noise, and viewers who never learn enough to enjoy the contest itself.

history: Sport broadcasting grew from newspaper reports and radio commentary to television and streaming, turning local matches into worldwide events.
competitions: Broadcast rights fund much of professional sport, with leagues selling rights and using the income to pay players, clubs, and facilities.
techniques: Modern coverage uses multiple cameras, slow-motion replay, graphics, and expert commentary to explain tactics to viewers.

title: The Suite Map: How All Sports Databases Connect
description: The suite map is a guide to reading the sports collection without getting lost in it. Start with the flagship, which lays down the shared ideas: what counts as a sport, how it is governed, how it is coached, and how it stays fair. Then follow the branches: team games together, soccer and basketball in their own depth, and the later families each in their own pair, from cricket and tennis to winter sports and esports disciplines. Where a topic already has its own home, other pairs point to it instead of copying it, so the collection grows sideways without duplicating itself. Cousins outside the suite, such as the teams, statistics, Olympic history, famous athletes, and basketball plays catalogs, are linked the same way. Sixteen pairs, thirty-two databases, and five hundred and twelve records in Wave 1, all marching toward a million.

demo.code:
print('Wave 1: 16 pairs x 2 editions x 16 records')
print('Total:', 16 * 2 * 16)
print('Flagship: sports; families: team, soccer, basketball, and more')
demo.expected_output:
Wave 1: 16 pairs x 2 editions x 16 records
Total: 512
Flagship: sports; families: team, soccer, basketball, and more

history: This suite begins with the flagship sports pair and branches into team, soccer, basketball, and later pairs covering every major sport family.
competitions: Each pair holds 16 records in two editions, and the suite as a whole marches toward a million records across its databases.
rules: Records cross-link rather than duplicate: a sport covered by its own pair is linked from other pairs, never rebuilt as a record there.
